For fishers like William Ortiz of the Little Traverse Bay Bands of Odawa Indians, the whitefish decline represents not just lost income but the erosion of treaty rights and traditional ways of life. Scientists are now racing to find solutions, including exploring whether native freshwater drum fish might help control mussel populations, offering a glimmer of hope in an otherwise sobering ecological transformation.

item.title: Kenyan teen leads charge on tree planting and climate awareness
item.description:
Baraka Moruri, a 13-year-old from Kenya, has quietly become a force in his country's environmental movement. Over the past four years, he has planted more than 7,600 trees with help from family, friends, and organizations, and he's set his sights on reaching one million before turning 18. His passion began at age six, sparked in part by learning about Nobel laureate Wangari Maathai, whose legacy of environmental activism continues to inspire young people across Africa.
Baraka's work isn't just about numbers. He's mobilized communities—organizing tree-planting events in schools, forests, and rural areas around Nairobi, and even influencing his grandmother to dedicate land to reforestation. In 2023, he led a climate walk with 700 participants who together planted over 2,000 trees. This year, his family published a book, *Go Green with Baraka*, encouraging African youth to take leadership roles in environmental protection. Despite being told he's too young to grasp climate issues, Baraka sees the evidence firsthand: erratic rainfall, confused planting seasons, and floods like those in March 2026 that killed over 100 people in Kenya.
This story is a reminder that climate action doesn't require a platform or a degree—just attention, commitment, and a willingness to start. Baraka represents a generation that will inherit the consequences of today's environmental choices, yet faces barriers to participation; experts note that less than 1% of climate finance reaches youth-led projects. His quiet determination and growing influence offer a hopeful counterpoint: young people aren't just stakeholders in the climate conversation—they're already leading it.

item.title: Drone captures rare video of 'magical moment' whale birth
item.description:
A drone operator has captured what researchers believe is the first-ever aerial footage of a humpback whale giving birth, offering a rare glimpse into one of nature's most private moments. Alex Forrest, a volunteer with the Organisation for the Rescue and Research of Cetaceans in Australia, was filming humpback whales off Kingscliff on the New South Wales coast when he noticed a female swimming unusually slowly behind her pod. What happened next took him completely by surprise: a sudden plume of red in the water, followed by the emergence of a newborn calf rising instinctively to the surface for its first breath.
The footage marks only the fourth time a whale birth has ever been filmed, and the first captured by drone. Marine scientists are particularly excited because the sighting challenges previous assumptions about humpback whale birthing behavior. Researchers had long believed these whales traveled exclusively to tropical waters to give birth, but this observation suggests the picture may be more complex. The solitary nature of this birth—the mother appeared to be alone rather than escorted by other whales—also offers new data for comparison with other documented cases.
This story matters because it reminds us how much remains unknown about even the most watched creatures on Earth. Despite humpback whales being among the most observed marine mammals, their birthing habits have remained largely mysterious. As whale populations recover and drone technology advances, moments like these help scientists piece together a fuller understanding of how these remarkable animals live. It's a quiet testament to the value of patient observation and the surprises that await when we pay attention to the natural world around us.

item.title: Country diary: In poet John Clare’s garden, I contemplate my ancestor who lived here too | Nic Wilson
item.description:
In the garden of John Clare's cottage in Helpston, a visitor finds herself contemplating more than just the gatekeeper butterflies dancing among wild marjoram. The small stone cottage, birthplace of the celebrated nature poet, once housed multiple families in cramped one-up, one-down tenancies during the 1820s and 30s. While Clare's intimate observations of this garden—his "affection's friend" honeysuckle, the red kites overhead, the twilight hours on his bench—are well documented in his poetry, the lives of his neighbors who shared the space remain largely forgotten.
The author has uncovered a personal connection to this literary and natural sanctuary. Among those cottage dwellers was Henry Howsden, son of a shepherd named John and his wife Mary. She imagines this distant ancestor as a young boy two centuries ago, playing among the flowerbeds and chasing butterflies alongside Clare's own children, perhaps absorbing the poet's reverence for "weedling wild" and self-seeded beauty. The garden, with its apple tree, vegetables, and herbaceous borders, would have been a shared outdoor room for all the cottage families—a common ground where nature and daily life intertwined.
This meditation reveals how a love of the wild can travel through generations like a quiet inheritance. The author traces a line from Henry the shepherd's boy through her grandmother down to herself, sitting now where her ancestor once played. It's a story that reminds us how places hold multiple histories simultaneously, and how our connection to nature might have roots deeper and more personal than we realize—sometimes reaching back through family lines to a cottage garden where a poet once asked butterflies to join the bees' delightful hum.

item.title: New exhibition tracing evolution of Māori carving over 700 years
item.description:
Te Papa, New Zealand's national museum, is preparing to open a sweeping exhibition that traces seven centuries of Māori carving. He Toi Whakairo: The Art of Māori Carving brings together 147 taonga—treasured objects—ranging from pieces created in the 1300s to contemporary works commissioned specifically for the show, which opens on August 29.
Co-curators Jana Pātete and Dougal Austin have deliberately chosen not to arrange the exhibition chronologically. Instead, they've placed contemporary and traditional carvings side by side to emphasize that whakairo is a living, evolving practice. The earliest pieces reveal Pasifika influences tracing back to Māori origins across Te Moana Nui a Kiwa (the Pacific Ocean), while later works show how the art form developed its own distinct identity. Among the highlights are pieces unseen in perhaps a century, contemporary clay work by Stevie Houkāmau, and karetao (marionettes) by Ngaroma Riley, including a self-portrait puppet called Kapahaka Queen that swings poi. Austin expressed particular fondness for a hei tiki named after Ruatepupuke, the figure from Māori storytelling who is said to have brought carving knowledge from the ocean depths. Pātete pointed to a tokotoko (walking stick) that appears to be a collaboration between carver and nature, shaped as it grew around a vine.
The exhibition offers more than aesthetic appreciation—it's a window into cultural continuity and innovation across generations. By showcasing agricultural tools, weapons, adornment, and puppets alongside each other, and by highlighting the work of women carvers, the show reveals both the diversity of the craft and its enduring vitality in contemporary Māori culture.
